paragraphs: The cadence is the release cadence: automated pass in CI on every change; keyboard and screen reader passes on every staged release before it is published; regression pass on every release that touches the components on the fixed-rows list. The time cost is *an afternoon per release*, and it is the cost of a store that does not silently lose accessibility a quarter after the audit.

The maintenance discipline — [change logs, test environments, rollback plans](/blogs/shopify-theme-maintenance) — is what makes the cadence sustainable. A theme that is tested like a product is maintained like one, and the two workflows share the same checklist.

The cadence is also the answer to the client's real question, which is never is it accessible but [how do I know it is still accessible](/shopify-accessibility-testing). The cadence is the how, the evidence is the proof, and the two together are the trust.

sections.heading: A sample matrix for a Shopify theme
paragraphs: A matrix for a typical theme starts with a short list of rows that cover the load-bearing surfaces: the main menu, opened and closed by keyboard with the return noted; the search drawer, the same; the product options, chosen fully by keyboard; the cart, from empty to populated with each change noted for whether it announced. Each row is a case, an input method, an expected behavior, and a slot for the evidence.

The next rows are the content surfaces: the product grid, with every image checked for a description; the collection filters, with the results announced when they change; the forms, with every error identified by field and problem. The rows are specific enough to run and general enough to carry, and the store's own pages are what make them real.

The matrix is never finished, because the store's surfaces are never finished, and a new section is a new row. The discipline is that the row is written when the section ships, not when the next audit finds the gap, and the matrix is the document that keeps the store's accessibility as current as its features.

sections.heading: Failing the build on purpose
paragraphs: The gate is the part people resist, and it is the part that makes the workflow real. A staged release that fails a matrix row does not ship; the row is fixed or, if it is a known limitation, it is recorded as such and the decision to ship is made with the limitation in writing. The gate is not a veto on the store; it is a requirement that the decision be made with the evidence in front of it.

I have failed a release on purpose — caught a regression in the staged pass that the live pass would have missed — and the release that was a day late is the release the client still trusts. The gate's cost is a day; the gate's value is the store that does not quietly undo its own accessibility.

takeaway: Accessibility testing is a workflow, not a tool. Run the same matrix on every release, keep evidence you could hand to a reviewer, and treat automated checks as the floor, not the finish line.
seoTitle: Shopify Accessibility Testing: A Repeatable QA Workflow
seoDescription: A repeatable accessibility QA workflow for Shopify themes: test matrix, keyboard and screen reader passes, evidence standards, and release cadence.

title: How to Maintain a Shopify Theme Without Breaking Storefront Features
excerpt: A release discipline for Shopify themes: change logs, test environments, rollback plans, and the test that decides when a change is a fix, a refactor, or a rebuild.
intro: A theme does not break from one bad change; I have watched it break from a hundred small ones, each reasonable in isolation and none of them tested against the whole store. The themes that stay stable for years are not luckier — they are treated like releases: scope stated, tested where they can fail, undoable, written down. This is the release discipline I bring to maintenance, and the checklist that makes it boring, which is exactly the point.

sections.heading: What breaks themes in practice
paragraphs: The failure patterns are a short list. An app update renders new markup that the theme's styles do not expect. A merchant edits a section in a way the code did not anticipate. [A platform release changes default behavior](https://shopify.dev/changelogs). A small change to a shared snippet lands on every page that uses it. A fix for one page's problem quietly reorders focus on another.

Each of these is invisible in the code review — the change is correct, it is just not complete, because nobody tested it against the surface it actually touches. The discipline that follows is organized around closing that gap: *every change declares its surface, and the test pass covers it*.
The patterns are also the reason maintenance is a discipline and not a task. A task is a change; a discipline is a way of making every change safe, and the difference is the whole job.

sections.heading: The release checklist
paragraphs: Every theme change, no matter how small, carries four items. Scope: one sentence saying what changes and, just as importantly, what does not. Change log entry: the same sentence plus the reason, dated. Test pass: the page types and interactions the change touches, run in a test environment. Rollback plan: what to do if the change misbehaves in production, written before publish, not after.

The checklist is short on purpose. It is the difference between *a change that is verified and a change that is hoped for*, and it takes minutes — which is precisely why it gets skipped, and why the skipping is what breaks themes.

The scope line is the most important of the four, because it is the line that catches the scope creep. A change that says I am only touching the header and then touches the header and the footer is a change that has already failed, and *the scope line is where the failure is visible*.

sections.heading: Test environments: the cheapest insurance
paragraphs: [The test environment is a development store or a staged theme](https://shopify.dev/docs/apps) where the change can fail without the customer seeing it. [The smoke pass on it is the storefront's load-bearing paths](/resources/shopify-qa-checklist): the main menu at every breakpoint, a product page with its options, the cart from empty to populated, and the checkout entry. The pass is the same every time, which is what makes it a pass instead of a wander.

The environment should also carry the realistic data the production edge cases live in: long product titles, products with zero images, collections with hundreds of items. The bugs that survive to production are almost always the ones the test data never had.

The test environment is also where the merchant's edits get tested, because the merchant's edits are a change too, and the code that did not anticipate them is the code that breaks on the day the merchant makes the change. The environment is the place where that change is safe to make.

sections.heading: Rollback that works
paragraphs: A rollback plan is only a plan if it has been true-tested: know which version of each changed file you are returning to, know what the merchant has edited that must not be lost, and know how long the rollback actually takes. The two failure modes are the rollback that erases the merchant's section edits, and the rollback that no one has tried, so it takes three times longer under pressure than it should.

The working pattern is to treat the live theme as a deployed artifact: changes go to a staged theme, the smoke pass runs there, and [publish is a deliberate act with a known previous state](/shopify-regression-testing). Publishing directly from the live theme is how rollbacks stop being possible.

The rollback is also where the merchant's edits get protected, because the rollback that returns the code must not return the merchant's content. The pattern is to separate the two — the code rolls back, the merchant's sections stay — and the separation is what makes the rollback safe.

sections.heading: Fix versus refactor versus rebuild
paragraphs: The three are different commitments and should be labeled as such. A fix changes behavior to correct a defect, and nothing else — a fix that restructures a section is a refactor wearing a fix's label, and it should be reviewed as the larger change it is. A refactor changes structure with no behavior change, and it earns its place only when the structure is actively blocking fixes. A rebuild is a new theme, and it is justified by a stated limit the current theme cannot work around — not by accumulated discomfort.

Labeling the change correctly keeps the review honest: a fix gets a defect review, a refactor gets a structure review, [a rebuild gets a decision review with the decision matrix from the custom-theme guides](/blogs/custom-shopify-theme-vs-premium). Each has its own evidence, and mixing them is how refactors smuggle themselves into release day.

The label also protects the client from the most common overreach: a fix that is really a rebuild, priced as a fix. The label is the line that keeps the three honest, and the decision record is where the label is written down.

sections.heading: The change log is a product
paragraphs: The merchant-facing change log is not ceremony. It is the record that lets the merchant trust a publish, the context that makes the next developer's job easier, and the evidence that the theme is maintained rather than merely present. Two lines per change — what changed, and why — dated, is the whole standard.
A year of two-line entries is a theme with a history. A year of silent changes is a theme with a mystery, and the mystery is what eventually gets the store into a rebuild it was trying to avoid.

The change log is also the client's trust document, and it is the one the client reads when a change misbehaves. What changed on the 14th is a question the change log answers in seconds, and the answer is the difference between a client who trusts the next publish and one who does not.

sections.heading: A year of small changes: the cadence
paragraphs: The cadence is what a maintenance year actually looks like: the app updates that arrive on a schedule the store does not control, the platform releases that change a default, the merchant edits that accumulate, and the small fixes that come from the client's own testing. Each one is a release, and each one goes through the checklist, and the year is the sum of the checklists.

The cadence is also where the theme's health shows up, because a theme that is maintained on the cadence is a theme whose change log is full and whose rollbacks are unused, and a theme that is not is a theme whose change log is empty and whose rollbacks are the plan. *The change log is the health record*.

The cadence is cheap in the right shape and expensive in the wrong one, and the difference is the checklist. A maintenance year without the checklist is a hundred untested changes; a maintenance year with it is a hundred small, safe, recorded releases, and the client feels the difference every single time a change ships.

sections.heading: When maintenance becomes a rebuild
paragraphs: The threshold is the stated limit: the point at which the current theme cannot work around the requirement, and the workarounds have become the theme. When that point is reached, the honest conversation is a rebuild, priced as one, [with the decision matrix from the custom-theme guides applied to the decision](/blogs/when-to-build-custom-shopify-theme).

The maintenance discipline is what makes the threshold visible, because the change log is the document that shows when the workarounds have accumulated into a limit. A theme that is maintained on the cadence reaches the threshold with a record; a theme that is not reaches it with a surprise, and the record is *the difference between a decision and a crisis*.

takeaway: Treat every theme change like a release: state the scope, test it where it can fail, know how to undo it, and write down what changed. That discipline is what keeps a storefront stable across a year of edits.
seoTitle: How to Maintain a Shopify Theme Without Breaking Storefront Features
seoDescription: A release discipline for Shopify theme maintenance: change logs, test environments, rollback plans, and the fix-versus-refactor-versus-rebuild test.
